uncited: Model Architecture Modifications define the function approximators (typically Multi-Layer Perceptrons or MLPs) and data structures used to map 3D spatial coordinates and viewing directions to volume density and color.
These variants set themselves apart by altering the input/output mappings, introducing hierarchical or modular components, or replacing dense grids with sparse/latent representations.

The core task of a NeRF network architecture is to learn a continuous volumetric scene representation $F_\Theta: (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) \rightarrow (\sigma, \mathbf{c})$, where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the spatial position, $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the viewing direction, $\sigma$ is the volume density, and $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the view-dependent color.
The rendering process integrates these outputs along rays using standard volume rendering equations.
**Position MLP ($\Phi_{pos}$)**: Takes $\mathbf{x}$ and positional encoding $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ to produce a feature vector $\mathbf{h}$.
**Shading MLP ($\Phi_{shade}$)**: Takes $\mathbf{h}$ and directional encoding $\gamma(\mathbf{d})$ to predict $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{c}$.
This latent code is trained using Iterative Amortized Inference and a ResNet encoder.
Reducing width monotonically decreases quality, while reducing depth first improves then drops quality if smaller than 2.
It established the baseline of using two MLPs to map positional and directional encodings to density and color.
Subsequent research has focused on modifying this architecture to improve performance, efficiency, and applicability to specific domains such as dynamic scenes, sparse views, and generative modeling.
